clinicalPearls: Regarded as a demyelinating CMT phenotype (a variant of CMT1) rather than a distinct disease, historically linked to variants in PMP22 and MPZ
Classic combination of a hereditary demyelinating neuropathy with postural upper-limb tremor and gait ataxia (dystasia)
Features overlap classic CMT: distal wasting, pes cavus, areflexia and glove-and-stocking sensory loss, with the tremor and ataxia being the distinguishing additions
The tremor resembles an essential or postural tremor and the ataxia is largely sensory, reflecting loss of large fibre proprioceptive input rather than a primary cerebellar lesion
Nerve conduction studies show markedly slowed motor conduction velocities in keeping with the underlying demyelinating neuropathy
Autosomal dominant inheritance is typical given the PMP22/MPZ basis
Diagnosis rests on the characteristic clinical triad supported by demyelinating electrophysiology and genetic confirmation
reference.pathophysiology: Roussy-Levy syndrome is now understood as a phenotypic variant of demyelinating CMT, most often associated with PMP22 or MPZ variants that impair peripheral myelin. The demyelinating neuropathy causes distal weakness and prominent loss of large-fibre sensory function; the resulting deafferentation of proprioceptive pathways produces sensory ataxia and contributes to the characteristic postural tremor. The tremor is thought to arise from disturbed sensorimotor feedback rather than a distinct central lesion. As in other CMT1 subtypes, repeated demyelination and remyelination generate onion-bulb formations and secondary axonal loss, and the diffuse myelin involvement explains the uniformly slow conduction velocities.
additionalDifferentials: Classic CMT type 1A or 1B without prominent tremor
Hereditary ataxias with peripheral neuropathy (e.g. Friedreich ataxia)
Sensory ataxic neuropathy from other aetiologies
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies showing demyelinating-range slowing
PMP22 duplication testing and MPZ sequencing, or a hereditary neuropathy panel
Assessment of proprioception and Romberg testing to characterise sensory ataxia
Family history and examination of relatives for the tremor-neuropathy phenotype
Exclusion of acquired demyelinating neuropathy when the course is atypical
Consideration of hereditary ataxia testing where the ataxic component predominates
redFlags: Prominent cerebellar signs suggesting an alternative hereditary ataxia rather than sensory ataxia
Subacute deterioration indicating a superimposed acquired neuropathy
Rapidly worsening tremor or ataxia out of keeping with slowly progressive inherited disease
New bulbar or breathing symptoms requiring review
reference.prognosis: Typically slowly progressive with long preservation of ambulation; the tremor and ataxia can be functionally limiting but the overall course mirrors that of other CMT1 subtypes with normal life expectancy.
pitfalls: Treating the presentation as isolated essential tremor and overlooking the underlying neuropathy
Attributing the ataxia to a cerebellar lesion rather than sensory deafferentation
Regarding Roussy-Levy as a separate disorder rather than a CMT1 phenotype
Missing a treatable acquired demyelinating neuropathy
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
